summary: Binance founder and CEO Changpeng Zhao ("CZ") stepped down and pleaded guilty in a Seattle federal court to failing to maintain an anti-money laundering program. Binance agreed to pay about $4.3 billion to resolve DOJ investigations, admitting AML, unlicensed money transmitting and sanctions violations. Richard Teng becomes the new CEO, and the plea terms bar Zhao from running the business and require an independent compliance monitor. The article also recounts related regulatory actions against Binance and Kraken.
one_line: Binance agrees to pay about $4.3B and CEO Changpeng Zhao steps down and pleads guilty to anti-money laundering failures, with Richard Teng succeeding him.
key_facts: Changpeng Zhao, founder and CEO of Binance, pleaded guilty in a Seattle federal court on Tuesday to failing to maintain an anti-money laundering program.
Binance agreed to pay about $4.3 billion to resolve the Department of Justice's investigations.
Binance reached agreements with FinCEN, OFAC and the CFTC and will credit about $1.8 billion toward those resolutions.
Richard Teng, Binance's former global head of regional markets and former CEO of the Financial Services Regulatory Authority at Abu Dhabi Global Market, will be Binance's new CEO.
Zhao said stepping down "is the right thing to do" and "I made mistakes, and I must take responsibility"; he will remain a shareholder and be available to consult.
The DOJ called the case the "largest corporate resolution" that included criminal charges for an executive; Binance admitted AML, unlicensed money transmitting and sanctions violations.
Binance collected about $1.35 billion in trading fees from U.S. customers, according to CFTC Chairman Rostin Behnam.
Court documents say Zhao told employees it was "better to ask for forgiveness than permission" and prioritized growth over complying with U.S. law.
Under Zhao's plea agreement he will agree to a recommended $150 million fine to the CFTC and make no statements contradicting his acceptance of responsibility.

Binance must prohibit Zhao from involvement in operating the business until three years after a monitor is appointed, and must appoint an independent compliance monitor and enhance its compliance program.
Binance launched in June 2017 and within 180 days became the largest crypto exchange; it had over $12.65 billion in 24-hour trading volume versus $2 billion for Coinbase, per CoinMarketCap.

The SEC charged Kraken less than a day earlier as an allegedly "unregistered securities exchange, broker, dealer and clearing agency"; the SEC had filed 13 charges against Binance and Zhao over five months earlier.
In April, Binance.US broke off its $1.3 billion deal to buy Voyager Digital's assets, and in August Checkout.com cut ties with Binance over compliance concerns.
